armF.prompt:
Below is a finished English news feature article (already translated from Japanese, no section headings). Write ONE short, natural sentence that captures the core of the story, in a way a listener can understand by hearing it just once.

Requirements:
- Exactly one sentence.
- Understandable on a single listen.
- Do not pack in multiple separate points; focus on the single most important point or twist of the story.
- Do not add any new fact, conclusion, or lesson that is not already stated in the article below.
- Keep who did what to whom, and what exactly it applied to, the same as in the Japanese source article and the Ledger below.

As a rough guide only (Trial-only guidance, not a strict rule): aim for one main clause with at most one subordinate clause, roughly 12-18 words.

Output only the sentence itself, nothing else (no quotation marks, no label like "In one line:", no Markdown heading markup).

[Article]
# Humans Show Up in AI Phone Calls. What Happened Behind the Scenes?

If you hear, “AI will make a phone call for you,” you might imagine that AI would be holding the phone, too. But in this test, a human concierge came out from the wings. It was the kind of twist that makes you look at the cast list and say, “Wait, they’re the ones who talk?” For some calls in Meta’s Muse, trained contract workers—not AI—made the calls and completed the exchange with the person on the other end.

The interesting thing about this story is not a contest to see whether AI or people are better. Who plays the lead role in the phone call? And what kind of information is handled behind the scenes? The spotlight falls on details like these, which you might miss in a description of the feature.

Employees worried that when contract workers handled the calls, users’ sensitive information needed to carry them out might be shared by mistake. But this is not a story about a large-scale data leak that actually happened. If we called this a “data leak incident,” the trailer would be more dramatic than the film itself.

Another thing in the spotlight was the question of what people were told. Meta executives admitted it was a mistake to start testing calls handled by contract workers without properly explaining this to people. The human concierge feature was rolled back for now. That does not mean Muse as a whole was shut down.

This does not mean that having people help is bad in itself. But if people join in on a task you asked AI to do, you would want to know who will handle it and what information they might be able to see. Maybe the main point this time is neither AI nor people, but the message: “Please tell us clearly who is playing which role.”

[Japanese source article]
AIの電話に人間が登場。舞台裏で何があった？

もし「AIが電話してくれる」と聞いたら、受話器を持つのもAIだと想像するかもしれません。ところが今回のテストでは、舞台袖から人間コンシェルジュが登場。配役表を見て「えっ、そっちが話すの？」となるような展開です。MetaのMuseでは、電話の一部について、AIではなく訓練を受けた契約スタッフが電話をかけ、相手とのやり取りを完了させるテストが行われました。

この話の面白さは、AIと人間のどちらが優秀かを競うことではありません。電話の主役は誰なのか。そして、舞台裏ではどんな情報が扱われるのか。そんな、機能の説明書きでは見落としそうな部分に、スポットライトが当たります。

社員は、契約スタッフが電話を担当すると、電話の遂行に必要な利用者の機微情報が意図せず共有される可能性を心配しました。ただし、これは実際に大規模な情報漏えいが起きたという話ではありません。ここを「情報漏えい事件」と紹介したら、予告編のほうが本編より派手になってしまいます。

そして、もう一つ照明が当たったのが「説明」の場面です。Meta幹部は、適切な開示なしに契約スタッフが電話をかけるテストを始めたことを、ミスだったと認めました。人間コンシェルジュ機能は当面ロールバックされました。Muse全体が止まったわけではありません。

人が手伝うこと自体が悪い、という話ではありません。けれど、もしAIに頼んだ仕事に人が加わるなら、誰が担当するのか、どんな情報に触れる可能性があるのかも知りたいところ。今回の主役は、AIでも人間でもなく、「その配役をちゃんと伝えてね」という話なのかもしれません。

armR.final_summary: Meta rolled back a Muse feature that let contractors handle some calls after admitting it was tested without proper disclosure.
armR.final_text:
# Humans Show Up in AI Phone Calls. What Happened Behind the Scenes?

If you hear, “AI will make a phone call for you,” you might imagine that AI would be holding the phone, too. But in this test, a human concierge came out from the wings. It was the kind of twist that makes you look at the cast list and say, “Wait, they’re the ones who talk?” For some calls in Meta’s Muse, trained contract workers—not AI—made the calls and completed the exchange with the person on the other end.

The interesting thing about this story is not a contest to see whether AI or people are better. Who plays the lead role in the phone call? And what kind of information is handled behind the scenes? The spotlight falls on details like these, which you might miss in a description of the feature.

Employees worried that when contract workers handled the calls, users’ sensitive information needed to carry them out might be shared by mistake. But this is not a story about a large-scale data leak that actually happened. If we called this a “data leak incident,” the trailer would be more dramatic than the film itself.

Another thing in the spotlight was the question of what people were told. Meta executives admitted it was a mistake to start testing calls handled by contract workers without properly explaining this to people. The human concierge feature was rolled back for now. That does not mean Muse as a whole was shut down.

This does not mean that having people help is bad in itself. But if people join in on a task you asked AI to do, you would want to know who will handle it and what information they might be able to see. Maybe the main point this time is neither AI nor people, but the message: “Please tell us clearly who is playing which role.”

## In one line
Meta rolled back a Muse feature that let contractors handle some calls after admitting it was tested without proper disclosure.
